title: Does Everyone Have Regrets?
metaTitle: Does Everyone Have Regrets? What the Research Shows
metaDescription: Essentially yes — regret is one of the most common human emotions, and the 'no regrets' stance is rare. Here is what the research suggests.
keyFinding: Nearly everyone reports at least one significant regret, regret is among the most common human emotions, and having regrets is a normal signal about your values rather than evidence of a wasted life.
honestAnswer: Essentially yes. When researchers actually ask people, the overwhelming majority report at least one significant regret, and regret consistently ranks among the most frequently named emotions in everyday life. The confident 'no regrets' stance is rare, and is often better understood as a coping posture — a way of making peace with the past — than as a genuine absence of regret.

Having regrets is not a sign of a misspent life. The research frames regret as a normal, even useful, emotion: it points to the things you care about and would do differently, which makes it a signal about your values rather than a verdict on them. What seems to matter most is not whether you have regrets, but what you do with them.
whatDataShows: Regret is one of the most common emotions people report. Reviews of the research, including Roese and Summerville's widely cited 2005 work, find that regret shows up persistently across people's lives and is among the most frequently mentioned emotions when people describe their experiences. Roughly, large surveys tend to find that nearly everyone can name at least one significant regret when asked.

Regrets are not scattered randomly; they cluster in domains where people had the most opportunity to act differently. Roese and Summerville's analysis found regret concentrated in high-opportunity areas of life — education, career, romance, and family among the most common — precisely because these are the domains where chances to change course are most available and most consequential.

Daniel Pink's large American Regret Project, described in his book The Power of Regret, surveyed thousands of people and similarly found that reporting regret is close to universal, with regrets falling into a small number of recurring categories. There is also a long-standing finding from Gilovich and Medvec that the structure of regret shifts over time — a pattern explored more fully in research on how regret changes with age.
whyItFeelsDifferent: It can feel like other people genuinely have no regrets because the 'no regrets' line is socially celebrated and frequently stated aloud, while the quiet, private regrets most people actually carry are rarely volunteered. You hear the slogan far more often than you hear the honest inventory.

Regret also feels heavier from the inside than from the outside. Your own regrets come with the full memory of what you wanted and what you lost, while other people's lives present only their outcomes, not their unchosen paths. So your interior sense of 'I should have done that differently' has no visible counterpart in anyone else, which can make it feel uniquely yours.

And there is a cultural script that treats regret as a failure to be avoided rather than a normal emotion to be metabolised. That framing can make an ordinary, near-universal experience feel like evidence that you, specifically, got something wrong — when the data suggests almost everyone is carrying something similar.
whatResearchSaysToDo: The research generally frames regret as information worth reading rather than a flaw to eliminate. Because regret tends to track the things you genuinely value, it can be used to clarify what matters to you and to guide future choices — Pink and others describe drawing on regret as a way to inform decisions going forward rather than to punish yourself for the past.

Treating regret as common and shared, rather than private and shameful, also appears to help. Simply knowing that nearly everyone reports significant regrets — and that they cluster in the same few life domains — can reduce the sense that your regret marks you out, which makes it easier to learn from rather than dwell on.

Where regret has hardened into persistent rumination or self-blame that interferes with daily life, the broader evidence supports working with a qualified professional. This page is educational and not a substitute for that; there is a separate, larger literature on how people actually make peace with regret that goes beyond what one page can cover.
whatDoesNotHelp: Claiming to have 'no regrets' as a point of pride often does little, because the research suggests it usually masks rather than resolves regret. Denying the feeling tends to forgo the useful signal it carries about your values, without actually removing the underlying sense of what you wish had gone differently.

Treating regret as proof that your life has been wasted is not supported by the evidence and tends to deepen distress. Since nearly everyone reports significant regrets, having them cannot reasonably be read as a sign of an unusually badly lived life — the universality is precisely the point.

Endlessly replaying a single regret in the hope of resolving it through repetition generally does not work either; rumination research finds that repetitive dwelling tends to intensify distress rather than produce insight. The constructive use of regret is to extract the lesson and redirect, not to relitigate the same moment indefinitely.
realNumbersInContext: The headline finding is qualitative more than numerical: across surveys and reviews, reporting at least one significant regret is close to universal, and regret repeatedly ranks among the most commonly named emotions. Exact percentages vary by how the question is asked and should be treated as approximate rather than precise — the robust part is the direction, which points firmly toward 'nearly everyone.'

Where the research is more specific is in the shape of regret rather than its frequency. Roese and Summerville found regrets concentrate in a handful of high-opportunity life domains — education, career, romance, and family recur most often — and Pink's large survey project found the same small set of categories appearing again and again. So the honest summary is: almost everyone has regrets, and most people's regrets look surprisingly alike.

faqs.question: Does literally everyone have regrets?
faqs.answer: Close to it. Large surveys and research reviews find that nearly everyone reports at least one significant regret when asked, and regret consistently ranks among the most common human emotions. Exact figures vary with how the question is phrased, but the direction is consistent: having regrets is near-universal.

faqs.question: Are people who say they have no regrets telling the truth?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, but the 'no regrets' stance is rare and is often better understood as a coping posture — a way of having made peace with the past — than as a genuine absence of regret. The research suggests most people, asked carefully, can name something they wish had gone differently.

faqs.question: What do people regret most?
faqs.answer: Regrets cluster in high-opportunity life domains. Roese and Summerville's analysis found education, career, romance, and family among the most common, because these are the areas where people had the most chances to act differently. Daniel Pink's large survey project found a similar small set of recurring categories.

faqs.question: Is having regrets a sign I've wasted my life?
faqs.answer: No. Because nearly everyone reports significant regrets, having them can't reasonably be read as evidence of a uniquely badly lived life. The research tends to frame regret as a normal, even useful signal about your values — what matters more than whether you have regrets is what you do with them.

faqs.question: Can regret actually be useful?
faqs.answer: Often, yes. Because regret tends to track the things you genuinely care about, it can clarify your values and inform future choices. The constructive use is to read the signal and redirect, rather than to deny the feeling or replay the same moment endlessly, which tends to deepen distress without producing insight.
